issues.legal_issue: An appeal filed after an inordinate delay should not be admitted where the applicant fails to give a plausible explanation and its account is contradicted by its prior knowledge and conduct.
material_facts: The institutional respondent appealed a trial-court decree more than four years after it was made.

The respondent’s officers had been aware of both the original and subsequent proceedings, had instructed advocates, and had received information about hearing dates, but did not ensure that the case was defended or that an appeal was filed promptly.
The respondent claimed that its legal department learned of the decree only years later, an assertion the Court found false in light of the record.
The opposing party filed a detailed reply to the delay application, but the High Court overlooked it and also proceeded on an incorrect understanding of the length of the delay.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s order condoning the delay was set aside. The application for condonation was dismissed, and the appeal against the trial-court decree stood dismissed as barred by time.
issues.legal_principle: Limitation serves public policy by requiring legal remedies to be pursued within a fixed period, while allowing courts to excuse delay for sufficient cause. Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the approach may be liberal for short delays but must be stricter for inordinate delays; no hard-and-fast rule applies. The same standard applies to private litigants and the State, although some latitude may be appropriate for the State’s collective responsibilities and administrative processes. That latitude does not excuse an implausible or false explanation. The Court relied on Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji; N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy; Vedabai v. Shantaram Baburao Patil; G. Ramegowda v. Special Land Acquisition Officer; State of Haryana v. Chandra Mani; State of U.P. v. Harish Chandra; State of Bihar v. Ratan Lal Sahu; State of Nagaland v. Lipok Ao; and State (NCT of Delhi) v. Ahmed Jaan. The application was made under Order 41 Rule 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

rule.if: appeal_from_trial_decree and inordinate_delay and applicant_had_notice_and_failed_to_act and materially_false_delay_account and high_court_overlooked_opposition

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decree: An institutional litigant filed an appeal against a trial-court decree.
predicates.inordinate_delay: The litigant filed the appeal after a delay that was inordinate in the circumstances.
predicates.applicant_had_notice_and_failed_to_act: The litigant’s officers knew of the proceedings but failed to ensure that the case was properly defended or that an appeal was pursued promptly.
predicates.materially_false_delay_account: The litigant gave an account of when it learned of the decision that was contradicted by the record.
predicates.high_court_overlooked_opposition: The court condoning the delay failed to consider the opposing party’s reply and relevant facts about the delay.

issues.definition: When an institutional litigant appeals a trial-court decree after an inordinate delay, had notice but failed to act, gives a materially false account of the delay, and the court overlooks the opposition, the delay is not condoned and the appeal is barred by time.
